name: Galena
toxicityNote: TOXIC: galena is lead sulfide. Do not ingest, make elixirs or handle without washing hands. Keep from children and pets. Wear gloves for rough specimens and avoid dust.
emotional: Builds a sense of weight and stability
physical: Kept nearby for calm and steadiness
Crystal healers link it to a settled, grounded feeling
summary: Galena is a heavy, silver-grey lead sulfide in shining cubes, a toxic display stone used in tradition for grounding, boundaries and sober clarity.
intro: Galena is the mineral you pick up and immediately feel the weight of. Its glittering, silver-grey cubes and stepped, mirror-bright faces look machine-made, and individual crystals can be as bright as new lead. It is one of the heaviest common minerals, and one of the softest, at 2.5 on the Mohs scale. Galena breaks into perfect little cubes along its cleavage planes, and collectors prize specimens from Missouri, England and Peru. Because it is lead sulfide, it is toxic when handled carelessly. Crystal enthusiasts value it as a heavy display stone with an anchoring presence.
history: Galena has been mined since ancient times as the main ore of lead and silver, with lead used in Roman plumbing, coins and glazes. Ancient Egyptians ground galena into kohl for eye makeup. In the early twentieth century, galena crystals were used in crystal radio sets as detectors, one of the first semiconductor applications. The name comes from the Latin galena, meaning lead ore. Today it is still mined for lead, and silver is often recovered as a byproduct. It is a classic mineral for collectors. Its use in crystal healing is modern, and mostly as a specimen.
meaning: Crystal practitioners see galena as a stone of weight, boundaries and grounded clarity. Its density is read as a symbol of stability, and the mirror-like faces as a reflection of hidden truths. It is linked to the root and third eye chakras, and used by some to support sober perspective and personal boundaries. Practitioners say it can calm frayed nerves, bring a sense of seriousness and help people stand their ground. Because it contains lead, galena is considered a display stone to be viewed, not worn or carried. Traditionally it is associated with feeling anchored and settled, a mood of quiet gravity.
howToUse: Display a galena cluster on a shelf or desk as a symbol of grounding and boundaries. Look at it for a minute while taking slow breaths and thinking of the one boundary you want to hold. Place it at the north or northeast of a room for earth energy. Do not carry it in pockets or wear it as jewelry, and wash hands thoroughly after each handling. Keep out of reach of children and pets, and do not place near food.
care: Galena is toxic and soft. Handle only briefly with clean dry hands, or wear gloves, and wash hands afterward. Never ingest it, never grind it, never use it in water or elixirs and avoid dust. Keep it dry, because moisture tarnishes it. Dust with a soft dry brush. Cleanse with sound, smoke or brief sun. Store in a labeled box away from children, pets and food.
identify: Genuine galena is very heavy, silver-grey, metallic and cleaves into cubes, with a lead-grey streak. It is often confused with hematite, stibnite and bismuth. Hematite is red-streaked and lighter, stibnite forms blades, and bismuth is iridescent. Fakes made of cast metal or painted resin exist, usually lacking true cubic cleavage. Galena is scratch-soft, so a fingernail can almost mark it.

faq.a: Yes. Galena is lead sulfide, so wash hands after handling, keep it from children and pets, never ingest it and do not make elixirs. It is best used as a display specimen rather than carried or worn.
In crystal tradition galena is used for grounding, boundaries and sober clarity. It is typically displayed on a shelf or altar as a heavy anchoring stone, not worn.
Galena is mostly lead, a very dense element, so even small pieces feel heavy for their size. That weight is one of the easiest ways to tell it from similar-looking minerals like hematite.
